title: Gwyneth Paltrow Is Very Sorry to Postpone Her Dinner
summary: Special and invited guests,I’m sorry to inform you that after intense public scrutiny, I have decided to postpone the Hamptons dinner I had planned this weekend to celebrate Sam Altman, whom you all doubtless know as the billionaire co-founder of OpenAI. content:
Special and invited guests,

I’m sorry to inform you that after intense public scrutiny, I have decided to postpone the Hamptons dinner I had planned this weekend to celebrate Sam Altman, whom you all doubtless know as the billionaire co-founder of OpenAI. I was so excited for you to get to know him the way I do: as a friend.

I met Sam last summer in a Sardinia beach bar, where, over a few rounds of espresso Sardinis (if you know, you know!), I asked him all about artificial intelligence—the sorts of questions heard at kitchen tables across the country: What does AI mean for beauty? What does AI mean for lifestyle brands? What does AI mean for being able to appear in additional Marvel movies without actually needing to be on set?

I knew you all would have questions too—the same ones, but possibly also additional ones—hence our little dinner. As the invitation promised, I had hoped to discuss these matters in an environment that was “private,” “off-the-record,” and “al fresco.” Now none of that is possible, except for the “al fresco” part; the lawn remains immaculate.

When commentators learned of the dinner, they immediately cast me—an artist!—as a “technofascist.” They made hurtful jokes about “consciously uncoupling” from the party, as if that is something that could be done without the assistance of a Kabbalist. They accused me of ignoring the risks of artificial intelligence and “sucking up to our new A.I. overlords” instead.

Of course I recognize that AI and its brilliant, visionary, amazing makers may be controversial—but I know firsthand what it’s like to court controversy with your devotion to making the world a better place; I see something of my own mood-enhancing stickers and bee-sting facials in Sam’s art. There’s but a hair’s breadth between slop and goop.

Besides, I believe that controversy is all the more reason to take a conversation al fresco. Is this so misguided? Is complete off-the-record privacy really so high a price to pay for open dialogue? I will use this lonely weekend to reflect, I suppose.

For those who have already traveled to the Hamptons, I am happy to provide for your return trip on my jet, the Jetney. Take some flowers too. I’d hate for the water to go to waste if it’s suddenly so precious. At least I’ll see you all at the Montecito house for the costume ball this fall. You are going to just die when you see Jeff’s getup as Daddy Warbucks.

Please also fill out the Google poll for a possible rescheduling of this dinner; I will endeavor to work around everyone’s Sardinia dates.

I think it’s only appropriate to close this note with a few words from ChatGPT on the value of dialogue: Talking to each other is not just a skill—it’s a superpower. Dialogue builds empathy, and empathy allows people to truly feel rather than to—OKAY, now that any reporters have tuned out, the dinner is STILL HAPPENING! Please meet me at my Amagansett DECOY HOUSE (you know the one!) for cocktails at 6 p.m., from which we will take the Jetney to my OTHER DECOY HOUSE (this one’s new!) for a seated dinner at 6:45 p.m. The flowers are already on their way!

Genuinely,
Gwyneth

title: Trump’s Bad Bet on Beef
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Three hundred thousand metric tons of ground beef are on their way to the United States. There’s no easy way to visualize 300,000 metric tons of anything (for context, that’s about 12 times the weight of the Statue of Liberty). All of that beef could fill an important gap in the American market—but not everyone’s happy about it.

President Trump announced last Friday that he’ll be temporarily lifting some tariffs on beef and that, as part of an ambiguous deal, the imports will be sold at “25 percent below current market prices.” He was likely hoping for a political win here: Affordability has been a losing issue for Trump and his party ahead of the midterms, and increasing the beef supply in an attempt to lower prices could be one way of giving shoppers a reprieve. But industry leaders immediately condemned the move, warning that it will do little to address the underlying dynamics that have driven up prices in recent years—and their allies in Congress joined them in the revolt. Now Trump’s on-again, off-again relationship with ranchers is becoming the whole country’s problem.

There’s no great mystery as to why American beef is so expensive. The steaks we get from the supermarket represent the end product of a long, multiyear chain involving ranchers, auctioneers, feedlots, meatpackers, and grocery stores. But beef starts with cattle, and after years of drought, the number of cows now grazing on U.S. soil is the lowest it’s been in 75 years. The return of a certain flesh-eating parasite hasn’t helped things, either. This, combined with the fact that Americans are still hungry for beef, has created a basic supply-and-demand problem.

Economists told NPR this week that the president’s move, which was made official on Wednesday, may shave only a small amount off what shoppers are currently paying for ground beef at the grocery store. It’s too soon to tell whether this will actually happen—the government won’t release its August data for another few weeks—but Trump’s announcement did depress cattle prices somewhat, which suggests that traders at least think that beef could become less valuable, as the president intended. This is a problem for ranchers, who applauded last year’s restrictive Liberation Day tariffs. Most of the beef that Americans consume is produced in the United States, and the duties had been helping prevent foreign imports from undercutting domestic producers; without these protections, meat-processing companies are free to buy the cheapest option, wherever it may come from. In a joint letter to the president, the heads of four livestock-industry groups expressed “deep concern” that the plan would undermine beef producers by devaluing cattle and would prevent the rebuilding of the dwindling herd.

Ominously, the White House has declined to say where all of this beef will be coming from. When asked which countries will be supplying the beef, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins told reporters on Tuesday that she was “not part of any of those conversations” and is “not privy to talk about that.” Trump mentioned that “a few” different countries will be involved but hasn’t said which. (Thirty thousand pounds of Argentine beef were recalled earlier this month over concerns that it hadn’t been properly inspected; the White House declined to respond to my question about where the beef will be coming from but claimed, without elaborating, that the plan would reduce beef prices while allowing the U.S. cattle herd to grow.)

Despite being a core MAGA constituency, beef producers and ranchers have been periodically annoyed at Trump’s tariff changes over the past year. What’s more unusual is that high-profile Republicans have also been breaking with the president on this issue. At least 13 GOP senators have publicly criticized the tariff adjustment to varying degrees over the past week. “Beef prices are too high for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small,” Senator Tom Cotton wrote on X. “I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider.” Others suggested that what Trump is doing is unfair, a way of rigging the market against American producers, who “simply want a fair marketplace,” per Senator John Barrasso. (Rollins seems to be supporting the current plan, though she reportedly opposed a similar tariff rollback in May.)

This isn’t the first time in recent months that the Trump administration—whose war with Iran has driven up consumer prices—has turned its attention to short-term solutions. As I’ve written, both Trump and Rollins have publicly praised business owners who have lowered their prices on certain goods, such as fuel and groceries. But these kinds of temporary cuts don’t amount to a lasting policy solution, and companies can’t be expected to shoulder this burden forever. The private-sector “commitment” to selling this imported beef below market price has a similarly short-term focus. The bigger issues remain unaddressed, and voters don’t believe that the administration has the economy under control.

The president attempted to make peace with ranchers this morning, writing on Truth Social that he’d give them the “right to PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD”—a nod to long-standing complaints about what farmers say is a monopoly among the Big Four meatpackers. But this olive branch is effectively just a promise to disrupt a different part of the industry. In trying to please everyone, Trump may end up creating even more beef.

The Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln Deserve Better

By Andrea N. Goldstein

When I was deployed at sea as a junior officer, I used milestones to track the passage of time. Each day counted toward something: a port call, when you get a break on land from the monotony at sea; the “crossing the line ceremony” when a ship crosses the equator (unfortunately, canceled at the last minute for my ship); and, eventually, the date I knew that, no matter what, I would be going home. Even on my worst days, that end point helped me stay focused on the mission and gave me something to be hopeful for.

The USS Abraham Lincoln left its home port of San Diego in November and was scheduled to return home in May. That did not happen.

title: How Karoline Leavitt Debased Her Job
summary: The lie is the elemental matter of the Trump administration. The value of lying is Donald Trump’s deepest belief. He built his celebrity image through shameless and constant deceit that permitted him to bounce from blunder to blunder while constantly reeling in new suckers. Lying is also what binds ...
content:
The lie is the elemental matter of the Trump administration. The value of lying is Donald Trump’s deepest belief. He built his celebrity image through shameless and constant deceit that permitted him to bounce from blunder to blunder while constantly reeling in new suckers. Lying is also what binds his loyalists to him: The highest calling of any figure in Trump world is to refuse any concessions to reality when Trump commands it, and the surest ticket to oblivion is to speak the truth.

All of this has made the job of press secretary in a Trump administration less, not more, important than it normally is. In most administrations, the White House press secretary has a unique role in shaping public opinion, whereas the other staffers are concerned principally with governing. In Trump’s White House, distorting reality, rather than trying to improve it, is the highest priority for every official, including and especially the president himself. In an administration where everybody’s main priority is to lie on television, the role of the press secretary is redundant.

Karoline Leavitt, who departed as press secretary this week, did the job perfectly well. But the job, as defined by this administration, is not terribly demanding. Historically, press secretaries engaged in “spin,” a now-antiquated term to describe the delicate art of arranging facts in the most flattering light. Spin requires real skill. Its practitioners must grasp the underlying reality, which points must be danced around and which emphasized, and how to walk a reporter from their skeptical premise to the administration’s desired conclusion.

Leavitt never engaged in spin, and she probably wouldn’t know how. Her method of replying to queries relied on the blunt-force repetition of talking points, however unresponsive they might be, sprinkling in heavy doses of personal abuse and slander.

[From the July issue: Use it or lose it]

Consider a sample of her style, plucked somewhat at random. It is the first item on a celebratory list of Leavitt highlights released by the administration—which is to say that it is not some unfortunate slipup but one of her proudest moments.

The exchange in question took place on January 15, 2026, between Leavitt and Niall Stanage, the White House columnist for The Hill. Stanage asked Leavitt how to square then–Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s statement that the department had done “everything correctly” with the fact that 32 people had died in ICE custody over the past year, 170 U.S. citizens had been detained, and Renee Good had been shot and killed.

A few lines of defense sprang to my mind as I listened to the question. If my job were to defend the administration, I’d reply that, yes, 32 people died in custody, but that figure says nothing about whether those deaths were caused by ICE. And don’t all police agencies sometimes detain the wrong person in the course of investigating crimes? If ICE is performing somewhat less efficiently than other law-enforcement agencies, maybe it needs more resources for facilities and training. A handful of facts and figures could have reframed this horrific scandal as a one-off failure amid mere business as usual.

Leavitt used none of these defenses. She first responded by asking Stanage why he believed that Good had been shot. When Stanage replied that he believed that an agent had acted recklessly, Leavitt savaged him as biased. “You’re a left-wing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in this room as a journalist. And it’s so clear by the premise of your question,” she said. “You should be reporting on the facts. You should be reporting on the cases.”

[David A. Graham: A dangerous new attack on press freedom]

Despite attacking Stanage for supposedly failing to report on “the facts,” which his question included, Leavitt’s reply did not cite any numbers at all. “Do you have the numbers of how many American citizens were killed at the hands of illegal aliens, who ICE is trying to remove from this country?” she asked, without producing them herself.

In the same exchange, Leavitt complained that Stanage had degraded the august profession of White House reporter: “You and the people in the media who have such biases but fake like you’re a journalist—you shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.” In reality, Leavitt herself, in one of her first and most important moves as press secretary, invited numerous opinion journalists and influencers to hold permanent seats in the briefing room alongside traditional journalists. So even if it actually were true that Stanage is “biased,” her complaint that this would disqualify him from the job would still have been at odds with her policy.

This exchange, in miniature, shows how Leavitt conducted her briefings. Instead of the journalists in the room, her audience was loyalists who require no convincing and who believe that any news story that reflects poorly on Trump is by definition a hoax. Leavitt communicated effectively to this audience because she seemed to be one of them.

For this reason, she will be easily replaced by another, equally effective functionary plucked from among the millions of Americans capable of the rudimentary task of responding to questions with repetitive, childish insults. In an administration rife with memorable rogues, Leavitt will fade into obscurity.

title: Welcome to the Scrolling Backlash
summary: Subscribe here:  Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube A lot of people are getting tired of their phone—they’re sick of the algorithms and overwhelmed by what can feel like a loss of control. The Atlantic staff writer Julie Beck dug into why and how people are trying to renegotiate their relationships ...
content:
Subscribe here:  Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube

A lot of people are getting tired of their phone—they’re sick of the algorithms and overwhelmed by what can feel like a loss of control. The Atlantic staff writer Julie Beck dug into why and how people are trying to renegotiate their relationships with technology. She and our colleagues just released a five-part podcast series called How to Touch Grass, and in this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Beck about why people are nostalgic for the pre-internet days, how our brains are changing, and the good that can come from getting lost.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Charlie Warzel: How does the phone make you feel? How does a TikTok binge make you feel, or even just, like, a before-bed scrolling session that we all have?

Julie Beck: Oh, sick. Absolutely sick. It’s like when the aliens get you, right? They take you up and then they probe you, or they do whatever they do, and then when you come back down, you don’t know what happened. It’s erased. It’s lost time. So I feel like I have emerged from lost time and like what happened during that time is unclear, but I don’t feel good.

Warzel: I don’t know that I have the amnesia part of it, but it promotes self-loathing in a way that like truly no other activity does because it just feels like a deletion of my one precious life.

I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain, a show where today we’re gonna answer a question. Maybe it’s even the question of the online age. How can we live lives where we use tech and don’t let it use us? This is the animating question of How to Touch Grass, a new podcast series by my colleagues here at The Atlantic. Over five episodes, Julie Beck and her co-host and producer, Natalie Brennan, explore what exactly is happening in this moment that has so many of us out there feeling like we need to renegotiate our relationships to our technology.

At the beginning of this year, I made a few predictions about trends that we might see, and one of them was that there would be what I was calling a scrolling backlash. That people are just really tired of their phones, of the algorithmic internet, of this idea that they’re being manipulated all the time, and that their attention is being directed towards things that don’t make them feel good or whole or happy. Now, as predictions go, this is a pretty safe one, but it’s really been borne out in recent months. These things are hard to measure, but you can just feel it out there in the world. In the artists who are asking that people leave their phones at home or in their pockets at concerts, in the genuine concern over whether younger generations are going to be able to read like older generations. And while the data-center backlash that we’re seeing right now is complicated, and it’s about a lot of things, including AI, I also see that as an outgrowth of this larger frustration about the role that big tech is playing in our lives and the way that people just feel this fuzzy loss of agency right now. It’s a loss that just can’t be separated from the devices that we use.

How to Touch Grass digs into so many of the ideas that I’ve been trying to poke at here in the first year of this podcast. Our motto here at Galaxy Brain is that we pay attention to where we pay attention, which also happens to be exactly what I found so valuable about Julie and Natalie’s work. And so I decided to bring Julie on here today to talk about this moment and to talk about what she’s learned in this series. How badly have our attention spans actually been fractured? How has she reevaluated her relationship to all of her devices? Is the backlash that we’re feeling and seeing right now justified? And crucially, where might we go from here? Julie joins me now to talk about it all.

[Music]

Warzel: Julie, welcome to Galaxy Brain.

Julie Beck: Hi, Charlie. Thanks for having me.

Warzel: So let’s talk about this. Let’s talk about the touch-grass moment that I think we are in. Even even the phrase itself, right? Why is “touching grass” something that people are talking about? And what made you want to just dig in and report on it?

Beck: Yes. So we had originally thought about calling the season How to Log Off, but that’s not as fun. But I think it also speaks to just a sort of general renegotiation that people are doing right now between how much they actually want to be on their devices and how much they actually want to be inhabiting the embodied world around you and the grass and the trees and the people and everybody around you. We wanted to look at like the various shifts that are happening both in the culture of the internet itself and the technology itself but also

the shifts in the culture of how people are thinking about their devices and how they’re talking about them, and how much they want to use them.

Warzel: Why did you feel like this was a project you wanted to embark on?

Beck: I have deleted and re-downloaded TikTok on my phone roughly four to five times.

Warzel: Nice.

Beck: And it’s usually like my friend ends up sending me a Lord of the Rings meme and then you click it, and to click it, to see it, you have to re-download the app, and they get me every time.

Warzel: It’s a gateway drug.

Beck: Lord of the Rings memes are the gateway drug kids. But no, I noticed something happening maybe six-ish months ago when whenever I was on my last round of being on TikTok, which is: Every time I would go on there, I would get nothing but reels of “how to be offline more”, like “how to live more analog,” “how to heal your attention span” on this app where I was actively in the process of degrading my attention span. So I thought that irony was interesting, and so I think there was a shift that I was just sensing within myself, but also in conversations that I would have with people in real life and in what I was seeing online of people really trying to just be on their phones less, be on social media less. And I was curious why now, when obviously we’ve had smartphones for a very long time, we’ve had the internet for a very long time, we’ve had social media for a long time.

Warzel: What is the answer to that? Why now?

Beck: Why now? I think some of it is that we’ve had it for long enough that the shine’s off the apple, right? And I think some of it is a confluence of these different bigger conversations. Obviously, there’s like a big push by many to get kids off of social media, right? Or there’s lawsuits against Instagram, and What is Instagram doing to our mental health? And so I do think that those things have leaked down in some way, but also even TikTok, right, has been pretty popular for a few years. We’ve had a few years of living in this sort of algorithmically optimized short-form-video environment. And it’s gotten to the point where maybe people have had enough experience with it that they’re starting to see the effects in their own lives and like starting to question that rather than just, Oh, isn’t this fun? I can watch Lord of the Rings memes. And I think combining that with the sort of arrival of AI on the scene, right? And seeing all of these extreme stories about people replacing relationships with AI, using AI as a friend or a lover—God forbid—I think there’s been a sort of opposite, if not equal, reaction to valuing more the embodied world and the real social relationships that we had. So I think people are reacting in part to the sort of evolution of the internet culture and social-media environment and the arrival of this new technology that’s really like getting its little tendrils into every area of our lives.

Warzel: So one of the episodes—to pivot here—explores nostalgia, which I think is a very big part of all of this hand-wringing that we are all personally going through, right? Is this moment different from others? Are we doing something uniquely awful to our brains that none of our ancestors ever did? And when you talk about nostalgia, there’s particularly a focus on young people who weren’t really around to have that pre-internet life. In that episode though, you have this moment where you describe a time that you got truly and deeply lost. And so it struck me that your co-host, who’s slightly younger than you, never had that experience. She’d never been an adult without a smartphone.

And so what do you think is the value of being in a place where you don’t have a phone to save you? Are we losing something when we don’t experience that vulnerability?

Beck: Yes and no. I do look back on it with a fondness. I would no longer—unless my phone died, I guess—I would no longer ever be in a position where I simply had to throw myself on the mercy of strangers and hope that they helped me. If I were lost somewhere, I can just follow the blue dot until I figured it out. And I don’t know that I yearn to go back to that. In some ways, that wasn’t very safe. I was like a young woman traveling alone in a country where I didn’t speak the language, and I had no idea where I was and no way to really communicate with anyone. I’m not mad that I have Google Maps and I have some sort of safety features to keep me safe when I go places. And I do think we have lost a little bit of something of just, kind of, being where you are and letting the experience be what it is. And those opportunities for connection, right? I would not ask someone for help. I would just use my phone. So I feel ambivalent about it. And I would say that, in fact, ambivalence is the primary emotion of the season and of just today’s technology.

Warzel: So there’s this stat that you reference—because we’re talking a little bit about people who haven’t had access to a life without smartphones—and I found it honestly just bracing, maybe even troubling, but the stat is essentially that 60 percent of Gen Z wishes that they could return to a time before everyone was “plugged in.” And nostalgia’s a very common thing. You get into this in the episode. Everyone has nostalgia for some period of time. But Gen Z’s nostalgia for this time before they were alive, it seems like something else to me. Like it seems like a genuine indictment of this moment that we are in. How do you read that stat? What does that make you feel when you hear that?

Beck: I take that status as not actually indicative of if you presented them with a time machine and were like, “You can go live in 1985,” that they would go in there and live in 1985. I don’t think they actually want to give up on all of the other things that have happened since then. But it’s just this sense of like, Something in my life isn’t working. I attribute it to this device, and it’s being expressed as like, I just wish we could go back. But I don’t think it actually means they wish they could go back.

Warzel: Yeah. I think one thing that I’m trying to figure out is: Do you feel like it’s just an escapist phenomenon in that way, or just a coping mechanism? Or do you think it actually leads to or has the potential to lead to a genuine backlash or push or protest against some of this stuff. I think about just the physical-media boom, like a push to do some things in a more analog way, even if it is kind of “niche” or “hipster,” or whatever you wanna call it.

Beck: Yeah, I feel like maybe I went into this thinking it is just kind of an escapist fantasy, in the way that somebody might be like, I should’ve been born in the 1920s. I would have made such a great flapper, or whatever it may be. But the expert who we interviewed for that episode, Clay Routledge, he studies nostalgia, and his whole take on nostalgia overall is that it’s about the future as much as it is about the past. So it’s not just warm feelings for the past and like, What a nice time I had doing whatever, but it’s also telling you something important about the way that you want to live now and going forward. And so, especially seeing what you’re talking about: the sort of rise in people buying physical media again, people giving up their smartphones for dumb phones. I do think it is inspiring some level of actual behavioral change. And even if you don’t go so far as to get a dumb phone and try to LARP your life like it’s the ’90s, I think it still tells you something important about what you value and maybe smaller shifts that you do want to make in how you relate to technology and how you set up your life.

Warzel: If there’s one real theme of How to Touch Grass, I think it’s that the tools that we use change us, obviously, in these unexpected ways, right? Our habits, how we see ourselves, how we see other people, how we talk to each other—everything. And the show explores this from anxiety to body image. And I wanna play you another clip from your own show here.

Sophie Gilbert: I don’t think anyone is supposed to see their own face as much as we do now. I think about this a lot, like how our ancestors would have felt like catching a glance at themselves in a lake. And instead we’re front-facing camera, front-facing camera, front-facing camera, and it’s weird. It’s warping our brains.

Warzel: That was our fellow staff writer, Sophie Gilbert, talking to you. What strikes me a bit about being hyper-connected is that, in theory, the access to abundant information that we have should be a good thing, I think. And it just doesn’t seem to work that way in practice. Like the way that we can learn anything, but we tend to gravitate towards information that confirms our biases, right? And pushes us deeper down whatever rabbit hole. Or how we can learn anything about our bodies and then it pushes us to go and Google these things that lead to more and more anxiety. The thing that Sophie gets at in that clip, really, is something that you hear a lot of people say, which is, We were never supposed to have this much access to ourselves, other people, information, and yet we hold that up as: That’s the beauty of the internet. Odell: And so I just simply stopped going. It was a totally unremarkable thing. I didn’t even tell anyone, Oh, I’m quitting Facebook. I just stopped going to it. And I think that’s really powerful. So that’s why I’m a big fan of anything that can give someone sort of granular control over what the—it sort of reintroduced choice in areas where people have never experienced choice. Because that, in and of itself, will cause someone to reflect upon what it is that they want.

Beck: All of this reminds me of a study I’ve been thinking of a lot lately, that found using an app that was similar to the Brick for two weeks had such a big effect on people’s attention spans that it amounted to, like, reversing 10 years of cognitive decline—

Beck: Oh my God.

Beck: —which seems really huge.

Odell: Wow. That’s incredible. I’m surprised and not surprised. Actually, honestly, this reminds me of, like, ecological restoration because when you restore a site, some things come back quickly and some things don’t, right? Like, you restore a wetland, some species are gonna come back almost immediately. The nutrient cycling of the entire site might take 100 years. Maybe our attention is similar in that, or our behavior, let’s say, it takes a long time to totally overhaul something. But at the same time, I think you might be surprised at how quickly certain things change. Like, in times when I was a little bit more embroiled online and using my phone a lot, and then I would maybe go somewhere, put it away for a while or whatever, I found that after a couple of days, I would notice that my attention felt different.

Beck: Hmm.

Odell: And by attention felt different, I mean I would notice details or small differences in things. It’s almost like having a higher-resolution image or something.

Beck: Are there other seemingly small changes to your routine that you feel like might have that kind of big cognitive benefit?

Odell: You know, I think trying to replace habits with other habits—I meditate in the morning, only just for, like, 10 minutes. I kind of calm down to a level where then it’s not going to as easily occur to me to then pick up my phone, or at least I’ll be a little bit more reflective about it.

Beck: Yeah. My thing so far, my recent thing has been taking up knitting and crochet, and this seems so small, but it’s like now while I’m watching TV, instead of looking at my phone, my hands are in hand jail, right? Doing knitting.

Odell: (Laughs.) Hand jail.

Beck: And it doesn’t seem so virtuous when I’m like, Now I’m only looking at one screen, but I feel like, you know, it’s an improvement.

Odell: I think that’s great.

Beck: Maybe I’ll get down to zero screens, TBD. But the other layer to that that I was just thinking about when it comes to phones and social media and stuff is, like, a lot of times where I’m going to learn how to do this new stitch or whatever is YouTube.

Odell: Mm-hmm.

Beck: So it’s not, you know, one is totally replacing the other, but there is sort of a relationship. Like now I am using that tool kind of for this other thing.

Odell: Yeah. Right, and I think that points to an important distinction, which is maybe a bit more nuanced than just, say, screen time as a statistic. You know, you were asking earlier about my changed relationship to my phone.

Beck: Mm-hmm.

Odell: I think about it more as like: When I look at it as an object, it looks like a tool. And it did not look like a tool to me before. It looked like a black hole.

Beck: Like a portal to the underworld or something.

Odell: Yeah. Or, frankly, I wasn’t even looking at it. I’m already picking it up. Like, I’m already in there. I’m already in that world. There wasn’t even a point where I perceived the phone as an object.

Beck: Yeah. You skipped right ahead.

Odell: Yeah. And now I feel like the things that I use it for: the Merlin app, it’s like Shazam for bird songs, I use that. I use iNaturalist. I use the Constellation app, voice memos for, you know, recording birds. That relationship, to me, feels really different because the intention and the purpose, I feel like I’m in control of that. I mean on my phone, the first home screen is all what I would call observational apps, so camera, voice memo, iNaturalist, Merlin.

Beck: Mm.

Odell: I’m kind of trying to remind myself of how I wanna use the phone. Like, I now associate my phone with those activities.

Beck: You write a lot about nature.

Odell: Yeah.

Beck: Being inspired by nature, how being in nature helps you, you know, pay attention. A common piece of advice for those who have been brain-rotted by the internet is to go touch grass. So are you also telling us to touch grass?

Odell: Yeah, pretty much. And, I mean, the weeds that I weed at my weekly project are grass, so—

Beck: And you’re touching them.

Odell: —actually, I’m saying Kill grass. No, I’m just kidding. (Laughs.) But the reason I think it became such a—that phrase caught on was because it’s just so obviously true. The obvious truth of it is, like, why it’s funny and annoying at the same time.

Beck: Yeah. What is it that you think the natural world has to teach us about attention?

Odell: Complexity, basically. Like, I think it’s a master class in complexity. It is kind of an antidote to the idea of the easy answer, which I think—I really blame Instagram for the oversimplification of political issues.Like, personally, that is just my ax to grind. And the idea that you could sort of absolve yourself by reposting something is just—yeah. It’s upsetting to me. But I think that there’s no easy answers to anything. Like, if you are a birder and you like birds, well, guess what? You’re gonna have to learn about trees.

Beck: Mm-hmm.

Odell: And then gonna have to learn about, like, seasons, and then, I don’t know, there’s just—everything is so tied to everything else, and there are so many things that are sort of, like, neither good nor bad or sort of arguable. We need lessons in that right now. Like, we need lessons in the sort of, like, Let me pick a point in space to look at, and then let me look at the context around that. Okay, now let me look at the context around that. And now you’ve sort of widened this whole ecosystem. I think the opposite of that is what happens online.

Beck: So Jenny, if someone is just starting to rethink the relationship they have with their devices, what advice would you give them?

Odell: Try to take an outsider’s perspective on yourself. I’m a big journaler, so I’ve journaled since I was a kid. So that would work for me. I would look at my phone, I would look at some stuff on my phone, and then I would just write down, kinda what it was and then how I felt about it. And I would be, like, brutally honest.

Beck: Oh, man.

Odell: Just pretend like you’re a scientist. And just talk to a friend about it. You could write it down, like, whatever. But, you know, I think there needs to be that, like, every so often you step to the side and you go, Okay, what did I just do? Like, Why did I do that? How did that make me feel? You can be super brief about it. Just do it for a week. Just see what it tells you.

Beck: Yeah.

Odell: Before you try to make any changes, because the danger is that a person feels shame, they feel that it’s bad. They’re like, Okay, I need to change this, and then they try really hard to change it, and then it doesn’t go the way they wanted, and then they feel more shame. And now it’s just, like, a spiral.

Beck: Yeah. I think especially with attention for whatever reason, it does feel very shameful, this like, Oh, I can’t focus; I can’t pay attention. I can’t even, like, read a book without having the desire to pick up my phone.

Odell: Yeah. And people think it means that they’re a bad person, and it doesn’t. You just gotta be patient and try a bunch of different things and maybe it’ll be more interesting than you think.

[Music]

Beck: Guys, huge news. Huge news. I locked my gym locker today. Nature is healing. I am the virus. For once in my goddamn life, I locked my gym locker.

It is day 13. I was on the computer all day for work because computer is where the money comes from. You can still screen fatigue yourself. (Laughs.) The old-fashioned way.

Captain’s log, the final full day of the experiment. Over the past two weeks, I read one full novel, I started two other books, I finished an audiobook, I crocheted a hat, I watched all of the first season of The Traitors. It’s not like I, you know, found myself with a magical abundance of time. I think it’s more like I just paid more attention and spent more time doing the things that I already like to do. That was time mostly well spent, so attention mostly well spent.

Brennan: Julie, when you set out to go on this experiment you got in touch with one of the researchers from the 2025 study, Kostadin Kushlev from Georgetown University, who agreed to go over the results of your post-experiment attention test with us. And before we call him up, are you nervous about your results, not so nervous about these results? Will it mean less to you if your attention span didn’t change on paper?

Beck: I mean, I guess I’m a little nervous. I mean, look, I am a nerd and I always wanna get an A+ on my projects. But I really do feel better, and if it’s just a placebo effect, well, a placebo effect is still an effect, right? Like, I’ll take it.

Brennan: Okay, I’m gonna dial Kosta up.

[Phone ringing]

Kostadin Kushlev: Hello.

Brennan: Hi, I’m Natalie. I’m Julie’s producer. I’m also gonna be sitting in on this call.

Kushlev: Hi, Natalie.

Beck: Hey, Kosta. It’s Julie. How are you?

Kushlev: Pretty good. How are you doing?

Beck: I’m doing okay! So, can we just dive right in?

Kushlev: Yes.

Beck: And tell me, before I started the experiment, how was my baseline attention span?

Kushlev: So your score was about three, 3.02.

Beck: Is that good? Good for a 35-year-old? Good, bad?

Kushlev: That’s pretty good. Essentially, you did about how our participants did. It’s a little closer to the level you might see in young adulthood or for somebody in their 60s. (Laughs.)

Beck: (Laughs.) Okay. Humbling. Humbling.

Kushlev: Yes. Yes. But, you know, but once we get to your post score—

Beck: Yes, let’s do it.

Kushlev: —things really change.

Beck: The big reveal.

Kushlev: Yes.

Beck: What changed?

Kushlev: So your post score was actually hugely better. So it was 3.8. And that is much bigger improvement than we saw on average in our study. So your improvement is about four to five times bigger than what the average participant in our study gained.

Brennan: Go Julie!

Beck: Write it down, Natalie. Write it down. (Laughs.)

Brennan: I’m taking notes.

Kushlev: Yeah. So you did really well on that.

Beck: Amazing, I think. Is 3.1 to 3.8 good? Have I reversed my cognitive decline? Or how would you characterize that?

Kushlev: You’re basically off the charts.

Beck: (Laughs.)

Kushlev: But it might take a while to reap the benefits of this improved attention.

Beck: Right. And it’ll probably go away if I just start scrolling Instagram again.

Kushlev: Right. Yeah.

Brennan: (Laughs.)

Kushlev: It’s certainly not a permanent increase. But I do like to point out that, you know, just taking a two-week break and not even a complete break from your phone, just sort of like reducing your use, can actually improve that ability to sustain attention. Our lives are just like so tied to these devices, so sometimes the question might be: Have we like essentially permanently damaged our, you know—

Beck: Yeah.

Kushlev: —brains? Like, have we changed our neurobiology and so forth? And so this seems to suggest that no, there is a way out. So it might be worth doing some of those digital-detox interventions.

[Music]

Beck: Thank you so much, Kosta. It was great chatting with you!

Kushlev: Alright, thank you, bye.

Brennan: Bye!

Brennan: Julie?

Beck: Mm-hmm.

Brennan: How do you feel about that?

Beck: Unbearably smug. No, no, no. I’m just kidding. No, I feel relieved, honestly. Like, even if the true effect size isn’t as big as it seemed, ’cause I am just one person; it’s not, you know, a full scientific study—

Brennan: Yeah.

Beck: —it still feels really good to know that it’s possible to improve so quickly.

Brennan: Right.

Beck: So it’s actually kind of wild that you can do something as simple as this and, like, bounce back so quickly.

Brennan: Are you going to keep using the Brick? Like, how are you feeling about—where’s your relationship at between you and your phone right now?

Beck: My relationship with my phone is cordial. We’re not—it’s not warm—

Brennan: (Laughs.)

Beck: —but it’s not cold. We’re cordial. We’re friendly acquaintances.

Brennan: That sounds like how people describe their exes.

Beck: Yeah. And, well, we haven’t broken up. It really is—it’s a situationship—

Brennan: Totally.

Beck: —that is ongoing forever. No, I’m definitely gonna continue using the Brick, and I have been still. Twenty-three hours a day? You know, maybe not.

Brennan: Yeah.

Beck: I have been Bricking my phone, at a minimum, before bed, so I can’t doom scroll right before I sleep, and I can’t look at my emails or Instagram the second that I regain consciousness. So that does help.

[Music]

But I would say that throughout this, I kept thinking about my favorite poet, Mary Oliver, and one thing that she wrote was, “To pay attention, this is our endless and proper work.”

Brennan: That’s beautiful.

Beck: So this season, I think what I’ve learned is: Your attention is your life. And I think on some level I knew that already, but after this experiment, I’ve really been feeling it.

Brennan: We started this season because we wanted to understand why so many people were feeling the pull to log off, right? We’ve explored a lot of the ways in which the internet can pull you into thoughtless patterns, whether it’s the way Instagram makes us feel bad about our bodies or the way that AI chatbots can send us into an anxious spiral. But it seems like what we are maybe actually looking for, right now, is ways to be more thoughtful.

Beck: Yeah, I wanted to feel more thoughtful about my life. I wanted to not to feel as much like I’m literally giving my life away to things that I don’t even care about. I wanted to stop nickel-and-diming the moments of my life away.

Brennan: Being intentional about where you give your attention.

title: The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
summary: Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were prote...
content:
Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art.  

Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists. 

You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama. I’m mostly a fan of her work. It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig. But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand. 

In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection. Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction. In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists. 

Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick. After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art. She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets. Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance.

Seymour Wally / NY Daily News / Getty
Yayoi Kusama paints Kent Feathergill in 1967.

Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy. They fought against cliché. They critiqued patriarchy. They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational. They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing. 

That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh. For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together. These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering. 

Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas. It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm.

But society got sick of hearing the alarm. And the kettle got tired of whistling.

Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973. Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death. The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio. 

[Read: An artist for the Instagram age]

Her psychic travails had to do with her upbringing (she had an authoritarian mother and an unfaithful father), which left her afraid of sex and intimacy. She suffered from severe audiovisual hallucinations, in which she would see flashing lights, auras, and dense fields of dots. She fell into deep episodes of clinical depression and attempted suicide twice. 

When Kusama reemerged as an active artist in 1989, she and her supporters presented her mental-health issues not just as an important aspect of her personal story but as part of the energy that fueled her artwork. All of this was healthy frankness, but it also undoubtedly enhanced her work’s reception. People could relate to the idea of creativity as a function of—and therapy for—mental illness. 

Kusama and her promoters emphasized the link, tapping into narratives about the artist as a suffering visionary that went back to Van Gogh and even earlier artists (including such figures as Piero di Cosimo, Caravaggio, and Rosso Fiorentino) whose artistic brilliance was linked to their strange behavior and (perhaps) mental instability. In the 20th century, the idea of a connection between creativity and interior turmoil was taken up with renewed gusto, and the category of outsider art (or art brut) was established. Outsider artists could reconnect us to the amputated life of the emotions, re-enchanting a world diagnosed by Max Weber, in 1917, as disenchanted.

Kusama was one of many artists who swam with these currents. She talked about her repeating dots as an expression of an inclination toward “self-obliteration”—an urge to dissolve into forever-expanding patterns. The idea sounded at once mystical, therapeutic, and nightmarish. The idea that it might be all three only increased her appeal.

Christopher Furlong / Getty
The immersive exhibition “You, Me and the Balloons” in Manchester, England, in 2023

This second phase of Kusama’s art-world success far surpassed the first, proving, among other things, that you didn’t need to be in New York for your career to go gangbusters. She became one of the most popular artists on Earth. For museums struggling with attendances, she guaranteed box-office bonanzas. 

Her zany, luridly wigged persona helped dismantle the intimidation factor that prevents many people from relating to art and museums. Her work’s upbeat vibes and instant recognizability (spotted pumpkins!) were huge factors in her popularity. They made it easy to let go of the idea that you had to have prior knowledge or be somehow “initiated” into art before you could enjoy it.

Jim Dyson / Getty
One of the artist’s Infinity Mirror Rooms in 2008 in Liverpool, England

But the speed with which Kusama converted her popularity into massive commercial success was sobering, if only because it seemed to signal her total co-option by the market. A turning point came in 2012, when the luxury-goods brand LVMH, under the creative direction of Marc Jacobs, incorporated Kusama’s polka dots into its clothing lines, adorning stores all around the world with her designs. As Georgina Adam reported in her 2014 book, Big Bucks: The Explosion of the Art Market in the 21st Century, the collaboration caused sales of Kusama’s work to take off and exposed her to audiences she would have never reached otherwise.  

From that point on, Kusama’s absorbing and fresh art, once charged by avant-garde energies, became more or less a meaning-free expression of market principles, an exercise in branding. She soon became a social-media phenomenon—the world’s most Instagrammable artist. Crowds waited in long lines just to spend 30 or 90 seconds in her Infinity Mirror Rooms taking selfies.

Kusama’s talk of self-obliteration sounds vaguely Buddhist or Taoist. But I suspect it’s more clearly seen, in the late phase of Kusama’s career, as pure capitalism at work—a function of the same logic relied on by Big Tech as it converts the liberating potential of the internet into addiction, polarization, and advertising revenue, and a drastic narrowing of human potential. You will no longer need an inner life, says this logic. You will no longer even be you. You will be data points and dollar signs. You will be ubiquitous, self-obliterating dots.

Kusama also achieved something that has eluded other artists who were co-opted by commerce and converted avant-garde energies into branding, including Warhol, Haring, Koons, and Murakami. The artist—an adorable maker of giant spotted pumpkins who lived in a psychiatric institution—became beyond criticism. You could no more criticize her than you could a grandmother giving a teddy bear to an orphan. 

Chesnot / Getty
The headquarters of the Maison Louis Vuitton in 2023 in Paris, France

I have almost always felt delight when I’ve entered one of Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms or encountered her pumpkins. But I smell something rotten behind their sameness and ubiquity. Successful branding is exactly what art at its best is not: a form of general seduction rather than specific engagement. I prefer the earlier Kusama, the artist of extraordinary boldness, who carved out thrilling new possibilities for art in a hostile, male-dominated field. For this, she paid a heavy personal price. But it didn’t stop her from making art that felt specific to her, art targeted directly at you and me.
